subtopic: PROPOSED AMENDMENT WITH RESPECT TO MEDICAL EXPENSES

speakeroldname: Mr. Stanley Knowles (Winnipeg North Centre) moved:
speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: PROPOSED AMENDMENT WITH RESPECT TO MEDICAL EXPENSES
speechtext:
That, in the opinion of this house, the government should give consideration to the advisability of introducing legislation amending the Income Tax Act so as to permit taxpayers to deduct from their incomes, before computing the amount of income tax to be paid, the aggregate of their medical expenses, as defined in the said act, rather than only the portion in excess of 4 per cent of the taxpayer's income, as is provided by the act as it now stands.
He said: Mr. Speaker, in rising to present this resolution to the house, may I point out that the principle which underlies it is already incorporated, at least in part, in the Income Tax Act. What this resolution asks for is that the implementation of that principle be extended, and in particular that medical expenses be put on a basis comparable to that which applies to charitable donations so far as income tax deductions are concerned.
I said that the principle underlying this resolution has already been recognized by the government. In saying that I have in mind the fact that since 1942 there has been a provision in the former Income War Tax Act and in the current Income Tax Act to the effect that under certain conditions taxpayers may deduct medical expenses from their net income before computing the amount of income tax to be paid.

Income Tax Act
I have already indicated that that right is circumscribed by certain conditions. In the main, these conditions are three. In the first place, the Income Tax Act defines what are medical expenses for the purposes of this deduction. The act, and the forms that are furnished to taxpayers, make it clear that one cannot deduct everything that he may regard as a medical expense, but rather only the specific kinds of medical expenses that are spelled out in the act.
I should point out that the definition of medical expenses has been amended from time to time since 1942. Each of those amendments has broadened the definition, but it is still true that there is a limitation; there are many expenses, medical in character, which people are called upon to pay but which are not included in the definition set out in the act.
The second limitation imposed on the right to deduct medical expenses for income tax purposes is the condition to which my resolution relates. It provides that a taxpayer may deduct from his net income, before he computes the income tax to be paid, not the aggregate of his medical expenses but only that portion of his medical expenses which is in excess of four per cent of his net income. I should point out that when this right was first written into the Income War Tax Act in 1942 the floor was five per cent rather than four per cent. It was in 1944 that the change was made to the present four per cent level, and later on in my remarks I shall have something to say about the circumstances under which that change was made.
The third condition that attaches to this right is that there is an upper ceiling, a limit on the amount that one can claim. For example, if a person has $2,000 or $3,000 of medical expenses in the course of a year he cannot enter all of that portion above four per cent of his net income, but only the portion above four per cent of his net income which is below a certain ceiling. The ceiling is $750 a year in the case of a single person and $1,000 in the case of a married person, with certain additions for dependents.
I have pointed out that there are these three conditions that limit the right to deduct medical expenses for income tax purposes. In my view each of the three should be reviewed. In my view the definition of medical expenses should be broadened. Likewise, in my view, the ceiling on the amount you can charge should be reviewed, and perhaps raised. It is my experience in this house, however, that if you ask for too many things in one resolution you do not get any

of them; so I am concentrating in this resolution on the limitation, or the condition, attached to this right, which I think is the most serious one, and I am satisfied that the taxpayers generally in this country agree with me.
I have raised this question in the house on a number of occasions in times gone by, although this is the first time I have brought it before the house in the form of a formal resolution. As I say, this matter hasi been brought before the house on other occasions, and when one does that he soon gets public reaction. I can say from letters I have had, from editorial comments I have read in various publications, that there is wide support for my contention that the four per cent floor should be wiped out and that the taxpayer should be permitted to deduct from his net income, before computing his tax, the aggregate amount of his medical expenses as defined in the act. So as not to obscure the issue, so as not to give any member from the government side who may choose to reply to this the opportunity to confuse the issue, I have accepted for purposes of my resolution medical expenses as defined in the act. In other words, the issue before us today is clear-cut and simple; it is just the one point, namely, that that four per cent floor should be wiped out, and that the taxpayer, in computing his income tax, should be permitted to add up all his medical expenses as defined in the act and deduct that total sum from his net income before he computes the income tax to be paid. I am not asking, in this resolution, for any other change.
May I point out, Mr. Speaker, as I implied in something I said a few moments ago, that in asking this I am only asking in effect that the same treatment be accorded medical expenses as is accorded charitable donations. I quite approve the right that is accorded taxpayers with respect to charitable donations. May I point out that when one enters on his income tax form his charitable donations, although there is a ceiling of ten per cent of one's income-in other words, you cannot give away more than ten per cent of your total income and get credit for that higher amount-still you are permitted to charge the aggregate right from the first dollar that you give to an approved charity. Thus a person, we will say, who has $2,000 a year income and has made contributions of $200 during the course of the year can charge the whole of that $200; but a person with a $2,000 income who has $200 of medical expenses can charge only the amount of his expenses which is in excess of four per cent

of his net income. The net income being $2,000, four per cent is $80; thus he can charge as a deduction only $120.
Now, that is just one example pulled out of the air. I want to go on and give at this point in my remarks three concrete examples, comparing what happens in the case of medical expenses with what happens in the case of charitable donations. Two of these examples are the identical examples that I gave on a former occasion; the other is slightly different from what I gave before. I have still others which I can give later on if there is time.
First of all, I ask the house to consider the case of a married couple without children whose income is $2,400 a year. The income tax to be paid by that couple under the rates as they obtain at the present time, the rates set out in the Income Tax Act, plus the twenty per cent defence surtax, is $70.80. Now, if that couple in the course of the taxation year have had to pay medical bills of $200, when they come to compute their income tax they will find that by deducting only the portion above four per cent of their net income they will end up by paying an income tax of $52.80. That represents a saving of $18; in other words, they get tax relief of $18 in respect of $200 of medical expenses in the year. But suppose that same couple, instead of having $200 medical expenses during the year, give away $200 in charitable donations, that same couple will find when they compute their income tax that they have to pay only $34.80, which, against the original tax of $70.80, represents' a saving of $36. Now, $36 is twice $18; in other words, a couple which of their own free will give away $200 get tax relief for that to the extent of $36. A couple faced with uncontrollable medical expenses of $200 in the year get tax relief of only $18. I submit that that is not fair, and that we are perfectly justified in asking for the same consideration for medical expenses as now obtains with respect to charitable donations.
Let me take another example, the case of a married couple with two children. Let us assume their income is $3,600 a year. The income tax for them at the present rate, without deductions, would be $240. Let us assume that this year they have medical bills of $300. So long as the four per cent floor is there, they will be required to pay $210 income tax, which means that they will get a saving of only $30 against medical bills of $300. If that same couple, instead of being faced with uncontrollable medical expenses of $300, were to give away $300 to approved charities, their tax would be $178.80, or a saving of $61.20.
Income Tax Act
There you have it again-a tax relief of only $30 to one couple for medical expenses of $300, and a tax relief of $61.20 to that couple or to any other couple if their donations are of the same amount.
I turn now to an example in a little higher bracket. Let us look at the case of a married couple with an income of $5,000, and with two children. Their income tax at the present rate, without deductions, would be $542.40. If they have $500 worth of medical bills during the year, their tax will be reduced to $474, or a saving of $68.40. But if that same couple give away $500 during the course of the year, their taxes would be reduced to $428.40, or a saving of $114,
I put the two side by side again:	This
couple will get only $68.40 relief in respect of medical bills amounting to $500, but they would get $114 tax relief in respect of charitable contributions of the same amount. My case is so clear one wonders that it requires any argument at all. Surely people faced with these uncontrollable medical expenses should get at least the same tax relief as is afforded to those who make contributions to approved charities.
May I point out, in support of this argument, that one of the reasons we need to extend this privilege by wiping out the floor lies in the difficulty that would be faced if one tried to avoid any definition of medical expenses. I have argued already that I think the present definition is too narrow. It does not include many of the drugs some people have to purchase. But, no matter what definition is arrived at, there would have to be some definition, and it would not include all of the things people come up against at a time of illness.
For example, extra help is often required. Food bills go up if one of the members of the family is ill. There are taxi fares back and forth to hospitals, sitters to look after children-and all the rest of it. There are plenty of expenses that come into the picture that increase costs when there is illness in the family. I submit that one way of trying to cope with that situation is to wipe out the four per cent floor and to allow the aggregate of such expenses as are defined in the act.
Another point I should like to make is that there are people who have heavy medical bills but cannot afford to pay off the total amount during the course of one taxation year, or during the course of one period of twelve months. It is a fact that, under the act as it now reads, a person can charge his medical bills for any twelve-month period ending in the taxation year. But there are people who are faced with bills they simply cannot pay off in one year; and when that

Income Tax Act
happens we find that those people lose even the small amount of tax relief indicated in the examples I have given.
For example, if a couple with an income of $2,400 and with medical bills of $200 require two years to pay off those bills-$100 in each year-then, instead of getting but $18 by way of tax relief, as would happen if they paid it all in one year, paying it in two years they receive no tax relief at all.
Similarly, the couple receiving $3,600, with two children, and with medical bills of $300 in the course of the year, by paying $150 in each of two years receive no tax relief at all. The $5,000 couple with two children, and with $500 medical expenses, and paying $250 in each of two years, would receive some slight relief, amounting to only $10.80 in each of those two years. In other words they would receive relief to the extent of only $21.60 against medical bills of $500.
I could go on to place on the record many more examples; but the point I am trying to make is that, in addition to the unfairness created by the four per cent floor, other aspects of the problem aggravate the situation. I recognize the fact that a perfect solution of the problem cannot be devised, but I do suggest that the government could go a long way if it were to accept the proposal I make, namely that the four per cent floor should be wiped out.
I see that the parliamentary assistant to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Sinclair) is working hard with his pencil over there. If he, or anyone else on that side of the house, is trying to think up some answers to my case, perhaps I had better ask if there are any objections to the suggestion which I have made.
The first objection someone might raise- that is, if he is just fishing around and trying to find something wrong with it because it comes from the opposition side of the house- would be the contention that if the floor were wiped out we would be giving greater tax relief to those in the upper brackets than to those with smaller incomes. To an extent that is true. It so happens, however, that illness is no respecter of persons or of wealth, and there is no reason why we should not be concerned about the costs of medical care for all our people, including some of those in what is sometimes described as the middle bracket-and even those in the upper middle bracket.
But the fact of the matter is that when you work out actual examples, the average relief in percentage terms which is afforded' by wiping out the four per cent floor decreases as you go up the income scale. The greatest relief to be given by wiping out this

four per cent floor is to those in the lower brackets. That is why my motion concentrates on that point.
But, just to trot this problem right out into the open, and to deal with it, may I take the case of the couple earning $3,600 and having no children, but having $200 medical expenses during the course of the year-which is the same medical bill I mentioned in respect of the first example I gave. My first example concerned the couple earning $2,400 and having medical expenses of $200. If my proposal were accepted, the couple having $2,400 and with medical bills of $200 would get a tax relief of $36, while the couple with $3,600, having the same medical bill, would get slightly more tax relief, or the sum of $40.80. The increase in relief is very slight. But may I point out as well that the couple in the higher bracket would still be paying $260.40 in income tax along with this $200 medical bill, whereas the couple in the $2,400 bracket would be paying only $34.80 along with their $200 medical bill. Thus the slightly greater relief given to those in the upper bracket comes out of the higher amount of income tax that they are paying. I do not see that that is any argument against the case at all. It simply proves that my case is completely fair, although the most effective help would be that afforded to those in the lower brackets.
Similarly I have worked out the case of a married couple with two children whose income is $10,000 a year, and have assumed the same $500 medical expenses as applied in the case of my example where the income was $5,000 a year. In the case of the couple with $5,000 a year and two children, with medical expenses of $500, if my proposal were accepted their tax relief would be $114 a year. In the case of the -couple with $10,000, with precisely the same medical expenses, if my proposal were accepted the tax relief to them would be $155 a year. That is not very much more, when you consider that the couple in the higher bracket would still be paying an income tax of $1,431.40 as compared with an income tax of $428.40 paid by the couple receiving $5,000.
In other words, the only argument that comes to my mind that anyone on the other side of the house might trot out against my claim is exploded when we consider these few examples and work them out as I have done.
However, it is also to be recalled that years ago, when this matter was under discussion it was said by the present Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott)-and this was back in 1044 when he was parliamentary assistant to Mr. Ilsley- that we should not go too far with this matter, that we should not press it too far

because, after all, it was intended to be just a measure of relief in a time of high taxation. I-t was not intended to be a form of national health insurance. I would point out that we are again in a period of high taxation and it is time to consider granting relief of this kind to those who are faced with medical bills. With regard to the other phase of what the Minister of Finance said back in 1944, may I point out that if we are going to have to wait and wait for national health insurance, in the meantime some tax relief of this kind should be afforded.
Having mentioned the question of health insurance in relation to this whole question, may I take just a moment to say that I am glad to note the suggestion regarding health insurance which was made in a memorandum presented to the government today by the Trades and Labour Congress of Canada. Pages 17 and 18 of that memorandum contain this interesting section:
Health Insurance
The greatest blow we could deal inflation would be to improve the health of the nation. Production is a pressing and urgent need. Illness, on the other hand, frustrates production, and poor health is the cause of more lost time than any other factor. As a defence measure and as a means of directly strengthening and protecting our democratic way of life, we believe that the early inauguration of a nation-wide health insurance scheme should be considered.

Might I just point out that I thought it was in order because I was seeking to answer the argument which was made against my resolution in August, 1944, by the present Minister of Finance. He said at that time that this was not to be considered as a health insurance matter. It was on that basis that I made reference to it. But I have made the reference, and I am prepared to let it go at that.
My reference back to 1944 prompts me to tell the house something of what happened on that occasion, and I do so to indicate the confidence I have that one of these days the gist of this resolution will be accepted
Income Tax Act
and incorporated into the Income Tax Act. In other words, I am bold enough to hope *that in speaking in support of this resolution and presenting it to the house, whatever may happen to it today, one of these days it will be adopted, as other measures I have fought for in this house have been adopted.
My reason for that confidence in respect of this matter, as I say, is what happened back in 1944. I pointed out earlier that the provision for medical expenses to be allowed as deductions for income tax purposes was established first in 1942. In that year the floor was five per cent of the net income and the ceiling was $400 single and $600 married. It was not long before members of the house began impressing upon the government the need of lowering the floor of five per cent and raising the ceiling. Indeed, in 1943 representations were made to the government that that be done.
In 1944, when Mr. Ilsley brought down his budget, it included two resolutions referring to the question of medical expenses in relation to income tax. I have in my hand a copy of the budget resolutions of June 26, 1944, and the two resolutions that related to this question of medical expenses were No. 4 and No. 5. I shall not take the time of the house to read them, but I would point out that those resolutions had nothing at all to say about the five per cent floor or the ceiling on the amount that could be deducted.
When those resolutions were debated in the committee of ways and means the question that I am now discussing was debated on the basis of budget resolutions No. 4 and No. 5. That debate took place on July 13, 1944, and can be found in Hansard from pages 4807 to 4816. It was a most interesting debate, in which quite a number of hon. members of the house took part. As a matter of fact it was initiated by the then member for Saskatoon, Mr. Bence. Several members of the Progressive Conservative party took part, as well as the hon. member for Cape Breton South (Mr. Gillis) and other members of this party, including myself.
Several Liberal members also took part in the debate. For instance, the hon. member for Ottawa West (Mr. Mcllraith) got into the debate, as reported on page 4808 of Hansard, and made the point that the cost of artificial limbs should be allowed as a deduction for purposes of income tax. He pressed his point strongly and was supported by other members.
Another hon. member who took part at that time was the then private member for Renfrew South, who is today the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. McCann). When the

Income Tax Act
minister was the private member for Renfrew South the chances are that he had the taxpayer's viewpoint a little more clearly than he has at the present time. At any rate, he made a claim upon the then parliamentary assistant to the minister of finance, who is now the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott), that funeral expenses should be allowed as a deduction. In that interesting debate he did not agree with everything the government was proposing, but, as I say, perhaps he was closer to the taxpayer's viewpoint than he is at the present time. He pleaded with the government to allow funeral expenses as a deduction.
As I say, that debate which took place on July 13, 1944, was quite interesting. It covers about ten pages of Hansard and was participated in by members of all parties in the house. They accepted the slight changes that the government was proposing in the budget resolutions but they called on the government to go further in connection with this matter.
During that debate I made the specific proposal that the five per cent floor which then obtained in the act should be reduced to three per cent, or preferably to two per cent. The then parliamentary assistant, now the Minister of Finance, debated the matter back and forth. He raised the question which Your Honour stopped me from discussing a moment ago as to its relation to health insurance and so on. I repeat, the discussion was quite interesting because the private members were pressing a point from the viewpoint of the taxpayer. They were urging the spokesman for the government to give consideration to the matter.
What happened? I have the evidence here. The budget resolutions in the form in which they had been brought in contained no reference to any change in the five per cent floor. However, as a result of the discussion which took place in- committee of ways and means- this is a classic example of the fact that debate in the House of Commons is worth while- when Mr. Ilsley brought down his Bill No. 180, to amend the Income War Tax Act, that bill included changes along the lines suggested, although he did not go all the way we had asked him to go in the committee of ways and means. Nevertheless, these changes were in the bill, even though they had not been in the budget resolutions which preceded the bill.
Section 4, subsection 4 of that bill provided for a lowering of the floor from five per cent to four per cent and a raising of the ceiling on the amount that could be deducted. I well remember the occasion and how the house was gratified that Mr. Ilsley had acceded to 
the suggestions made on the floor of the house, at least to the extent that he had gone. He did not go as far as we asked, but at least he recognized in principle that our claim was just and that the floor should be lowered and the ceiling raised.
As a result of that action by the government they were complimented from this side of the house. In fact, I did not hesitate to pay them a compliment myself. I find that on August 7, 1944, as recorded on page 6409 of Hansard, the then parliamentary assistant to the Minister of Finance moved the second reading of Bill No. 180, to amend the Income War Tax Act. I was given the floor immediately and I commended the government for the various changes that had been made in the bill consequent upon the disoussion in committee of ways and means. I complimented the government for its proposal to drop the floor from five per cent down to four per cent.
That was on Monday, August 7, 1944. At the close of that afternoon we reached section 4, subsection 4 of the amending bill, and I should like to quote this interesting paragraph of a statement by -the present Minister of Finance, as reported on page 6072 of Hansard:

The hon. member for Winnipeg
North Centre has already spoken about this. This is a clause where, in spite of charges to the contrary, the government has not only listened to representations which have been made by all sides of the house but acceded to them in some respects. If the committee will bear with me for a moment- it is one minute to six o'clock-I should like to conclude this section. The government has done this in three ways.
The then parliamentary assistant to the Minister of Finance went on to point out that the bill lowered the floor from five per cent to four per cent, increased the upper limits from $400 to $600 and from $600 to $900, and broadened the provisions with respect to medical expenses to include artificial limbs and certain other items of that kind. The result of that was, of course, that the subsection was agreed to immediately. The house was extremely pleased that the debate had been worth while, and that the government had accepted our suggestions, at least in part.
It is in that spirit, Mr. Speaker, that I present this motion to the house today. I am conscious of the fact that this year's budget will be brought down in less than two weeks, on Tuesday, April 8. But there is still time for the government to give consideration to this point. I do not think there is any argument against it. I believe the people of Canada wholeheartedly support this proposal, and I think they deserve it. I present it in

the name of fairness, and out of consideration to the burdens that medical expenses place upon our people. I hope that steps will be taken immediately to wipe out this four per cent floor and permit taxpayers, when they compute their income taxes, to deduct not just their medical expenses above four per cent of their net income but the whole of their medical expenses as defined in the act.

I am delighted that the member for Simcoe North (Mr. Ferguson) is back in the house. I hope he will listen carefully, and give us all the benefit of the very apt interruptions on which he prides himself.
This resolution asks the Minister of Finance to give consideration to a certain proposal. At this time of year the minister is asked to give consideration to many proposals, and that is the proper democratic way for the people of this country, either as individuals or as groups, or acting through their members of parliament, to call the attention of the minister to changes which they believe to be desirable in our taxation system. These requests to the minister may take the form of letters, the most common way; of interviews, and many of the members of this house have participated in interviews concerning some problem in their riding; or of actual resolutions in this house such as the present one.
Now, of course, as the date of the budget draws near, is the time of year when we receive the most requests, but I think there is no time of the year when the Minister of Finance is not giving consideration to briefs, letters or interviews asking for tax changes. I believe the degree of consideration depends
Income Tax Act
upon several things. The first is the feasibility and practicability of the actual proposal made. Second, and a thing which must never be forgotten, is the effect upon revenues. After all, the purpose of taxes in this country is to raise revenues for those national projects and services which the people, and certain members of parliament, are not at all backward about putting forward.
Last night, for example, we heard a Pacific pact suggested for the second time by an opposition member. The Atlantic pact is costing us about $2 billion a year, so I imagine a Pacific pact would cost about the same amount. No mention was made, of course, of the fact that taxes would have to be greatly raised to meet that enormous extra expense.

speechtext:
The next is a minor point, but it is the type of approach through which the proposal is made. We, of course, remember the minister reading a circular letter to automobile dealers in which they were urged to lobby members of parliament, not to burden or confuse the poor stupid members with too many facts or figures, and to offer free publicity over the radio or through the newspapers for the members who went along that way. That is a type of approach very different from the type of approach when members of parliament, trade groups and citizens bring forward, as they should, in direct and straight-forward fashion, the tax problems which they feel the minister should consider. This is the position in which the minister finds himself in the last two or three months before the presentation of the budget, and that activity-the considering of various proposals-is at its peak today.
This resolution asks the minister to give consideration to extending the present exemption for medical expenses. Each year when I take my part in putting through the budget resolutions I encounter this demand from members for the extension of exemptions. There are some fundamental rules so far as tax laws are concerned. Taxes should be equitable; they should be reasonable; they should be understood, and, from the administration point of view, they must be effective in that there can be effective collection from everybody. Then, the cost of collection must not be exorbitant so that too much of the revenue is lost in administration. In general I submit that special exemptions violate almost all of these principles. I believe most of us would agree that, in theory at least, a single tax based on gross income would be the easiest understood income tax and the easiest from an administrative point

Income Tax Act
of view. It would of course need different rates from those applicable under our present tax. It might not be as equitable as a system with certain basic exemptions, but once you introduce exemptions you add an element to the tax laws which gives rise to misunderstandings as far as the taxpayers are concerned.
Perhaps I can explain by referring to the United States system of personal income tax, because it has been referred to here. They have so many special exemptions that the ordinary individual almost requires a tax consultant to help fill out his personal tax form. There is always that gnawing fear in an individual that he has not included an exemption that he does not know about. I believe that is a great argument for having our tax laws as simple as possible, so all the taxpayers understand all their rights. When we come to the matter of exemptions, to try to bring an extra degree of equitability to our tax structure, we must first of all agree that we cannot give special individual exemptions in a national taxation system. Any exemption must be on a broad national basis. When we give such broad national exemptions the immediate result, of course, must be that we lose a substantial amount of revenue. Tax revenues must always be matched against the expenditures which this parliament votes, so this loss must be regained elsewhere.
This year we are faced with meeting a total bill of $4,300 million. Any tax exemption now given to any special group must therefore be compensated for by an increase in taxes elsewhere. Most of us in our municipalities are well aware of this problem. When people ask for a lower assessment and lower assessments are given, the mill rate must go up because the municipal authority must And the revenue out of taxes to operate the municipality. The other point about exemptions is that once you get into the field of exemptions, once you break that easily defined margin, then one exemption leads to another. The exemption before us today is an excellent example of the course of an exemption in our tax laws. The member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) wants this exemption extended so that it would be more like the charitable donations exemption.
When this exemption was introduced in 1942, it was regarded as a generous and progressive step forward. Incidentally, it was not brought in at the demand of members of parliament or of any large group in this country. It was actually put forward by one of the officials of the Department of Finance. The minister at that time, Mr. Ilsley, was extremely concerned about the heavy impact of war taxes. The member for

Winnipeg North Centre mentioned that in his speech. In those days we had a thirty per cent initial tax on income above $1,500 for a married man, as against an initial tax of eighteen per cent plus old age security on income above $2,000 for a married man today. We had compulsory savings as well as the patriotic drive for the purchase of war bonds. All these measures siphoned off purchasing power, and laid an extremely heavy burden on the salary of the little man. As a consequence he was extremely vulnerable to unusual expenses, the most common of which is the hazard of sickness which can strike any family at any time. It was for that reason that this official suggested that an exemption of expenses above the average medical costs across this country should be given. This average ran to between five and six per cent. It was thought that an exemption of five per cent was on the generous side, because the lower you have these exemptions the more generous you are, and such an exemption was given in the budget of that year.
However, a ceiling was put on the amount which could be so deducted, and, as the member for Winnipeg North Centre said, it was $400 for a single man and $600 for a married man with $100 for each child up to four. This made a total exemption for a married man and family of $1,000. As I have said if you read Hansard of that day you will find that members in every part of the house welcomed this generous, progressive step. Members of parliament themselves, however, are progressive because the next year it was not good enough. Requests were made to extend this exemption to cover the cost of drugs bought direct from the drugstore. Drugs that were used in the hospital were put on the hospital bill and so were already deductible. There was resistance to this request because many of the patent medicines which people may buy may have a dubious effect, though some are of great benefit. Then, there is the problem of administration. It makes it difficult for the administrative body, the officials of the Department of National Revenue, to check an endless stream of receipts for small expenditures made at the local drugstore.
However, pressure persisted and in 1944 the first major changes were made in this exemption. The rate of exemption was reduced from five per cent to four per cent in order to cover in an easily managed way, with no necessity for receipts or check of receipts, this matter of drug costs. The house was pleased with that, and thought it a good solution. Then, the maximum amounts which could be deducted were raised to $600 and

$900 in 1944, making the maximum exemption for a family man with four dependents $1,500. We lowered the exemption from five per cent to four per cent primarily to cover local purchases in drugstores, and then raised the top limit of allowable deductions. We also extended the period in which expenses are incurred to cover not just the actual calendar year for which income tax is assessed. For example, a man might have an unusual expense extending for four months of one year and six months of another; but since our personal income tax is not carried backward and forward, he would then have it divided between two tax returns, although the bill will come to him and have to be paid at one time; so that provision was made that in a single tax return a period of twelve months bills incurred across two calendar years, could be included as a single item for that return. There could also be included the cost of an attendant who had to be in waiting on a sick person for twelve months of the year. Finally-and this was probably the major change-we agreed to include the costs of medical care and hospital care outside of Canada. That was a major step forward, not so far as the person is concerned but as far as the administration is concerned, because the Department of National Revenue obviously have great difficulty in checking the validity of receipts from foreign countries where we have no administrative staffs.
The next year we had still more changes. We allowed the charges to be made against the estate of a man who had died after illness; and later, the following year, we included certain surgical appliances and wheel chairs as deductible costs.
Then in 1949, again because of pressure by members, and because of pressure by groups -and when I say pressure, I mean perfectly proper pressure; I suppose "representations" would be a better word-the top of the exemption was raised from $750 to $1,000, with $250 for each child, so that the top exemptions for a married man is now $2,000. Then last year we made a still further step forward in allowing the deduction of specially expensive drugs on prescriptions. They are listed in section 26 of the Income Tax Act and include insulin, cortisone, and liver extract for pernicious anaemia. Hon. members will recall that at that time there was also the request that other expensive drugs be included. It was, of course, pointed out that the first drop from five per cent to four per cent was intended to cover the cost of drugs without the necessity of a detailed check of receipts by the Department of National Revenue.
Income Tax Act
Then we come to the problem today in connection with the resolution of the hon. member. The first question to be asked is this: Is the problem of unusual medical expenses incurred by wage earners increasing or diminishing. From a study of our records I would say that the problem of this hazard, caused by prolonged sickness imposing undue financial strain on the average budget, is diminishing over the years because of the introduction of hospital insurance in Saskatchewan and British Columbia, because of the extension of many company health insurance schemes to cover not only the employee but his family, because of the extension of community schemes like Blue Cross and because of the increased sale through private insurance companies of health and accident insurance. But that decrease raises a point as to why this hazard of unusual medical expenses is allowed as a deduction, while other hazards are not included, such as that of fire or flood or tornado whereby the ordinary wage earner can lose his main capital, his home, just as quickly as he can lose his income from sickness. So far we have said that a man should cover himself against unusual medical expenses is by insurance-without	saying whether that
doubtedly will come demands, as the years go by, for including these unusual expenses in the class of exemptions.
This, of course, raises the point as to whether or not we should try to do indirectly through tax relief things which are better done directly in other ways. It is a problem which arises in connection with every single tax exemption asked for in this house. The hon. member mentioned it briefly but was called to order by the Speaker, so I will not get far into that field. But I think that the logical way for a person to protect himself against unusual medical expenses is by insurance-without saying whether that insurance should be private insurance, company plan insurance or state insurance-just in the same way as most people today cover themselves against the hazard of losing their home and belongings by fire.
Since the last budget, many representations have been made to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott), and he has studied them. I think perhaps some measure of the necessity for tax changes in any field can be gathered by the amount of correspondence, interviews and briefs which the tax department receives during the course of the year. If that is true, then I would say that the correspondence on this matter of medical expenses received during the last year by the Minister of Finance would indicate a fairly high degree of acceptance of the present

Income Tax Act
regulations. We have received only three briefs-they were from the Canadian Congress of Labour, the Canadian Federation of Agriculture and the Canadian Medical Association-asking in a variety of ways for improvements in the present exemptions. We have received formal letters from six government members and two Conservative members asking relief on behalf of some constituent who had had a heavy burden of medical expenses, and suggesting that further relief should be given in the next budget. I know that quite a number of members of all parties as well have spoken either to the Minister of Finance or to myself with regard to this matter.
A variety of proposals have been put forward to the Minister of Finance and to the budget committee and they have already been considered by them, are being considered today and will be considered again before the budget is brought down on April 8. I perhaps could touch on the two or three major ones.
The first suggestion is part of the suggestion made by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre: Why do we not remove the four per cent average entirely? There are two or three fairly good reasons for that. First of all, four per cent is quite a bit less than the average medical and hospital expenses across this nation, so we are giving some allowance even to average costs. Our main tax exemptions of $2,000 for a married man and $1,000 for a single man are in part to cover usual expenses, such as the usual expenses of food, clothing and transportation. This specific exemption we are now discussing was put in for unusual expenses. Once that door was opened, then of course there would be demands for exemptions of other unusual amounts in the ordinary man's budget. The hon. member for Spadina (Mr. Croll) raised this proposal of removing or lowering the four per cent item, and pointed out that this would give the maximum help to the little man, the man with just enough income to place him in the income tax bracket.
A point-which I mentioned in the beginning-is the fact that this tax must not only be good in theory and good in the House of Commons but must be good in practice as far as the Department of National Revenue is concerned in the collection of the tax and in the verification that there is no abuse through fraud or evasion. When you expect the department to attempt to verify and spot check the endless amount of small bills which will be turned in if all medical expenses are to be deducted, you are imposing on them a large administrative task, and a costly one by reason of the salaries of civil

servants who would have to be employed for what would be a comparatively small tax relief.
A third objection is the fact that in most of these medical schemes it has been found necessary-whether it be a state scheme, a company scheme, or a private scheme-to place some sort of check against too free use, which actually becomes abuse, of the facilities offered. For example, in British Columbia, in connection with the hospital insurance they have had to bring in coinsurance, a small initial charge in hospitals to prevent unnecessary use of hospital beds. Most of the company health insurance schemes in my riding insist that a man pay half the cost of drugs, again to prevent abuse and waste of drugs if provided free. Most of them too make the request for a small payment from the man on his first visit or on his family's first visit to a doctor to check waste of the doctor's time with trivial visits. I think perhaps this present four per cent is in that category, of a check on unnecessary expenditures.
The second proposal raised was this: Why do we not change the top limit and make it a percentage of income on the top as well as on the bottom? For example, deductions not to exceed ten per cent of the taxpayer's income. I think, if that were done, it would of course be of most benefit to those who were in the upper brackets. There is, of course, nothing against that, except that it is a complete reversal of our basic philosophy as far as income tax is concerned, according to which taxes are based on ability to pay, so the higher the income the more the tax payment.
Then the third proposal is that the time has come to raise the present ceiling again. We have raised the ceiling twice now from $400 to $500 to $750 for the single man and from $500 to $750 to $1,000 for the married man. In view of the increased medical costs and fees, increased hospital charges, and increased cost of drugs, perhaps the time has come to raise that level. Then finally there is the proposal of the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre to remove the present top ceiling on deductions completely. I have been discussing this tax from two points of view, namely the actual effect of the tax when levied, and second, the actual administration: Is it feasible and practical? There is certainly no objection to that proposal from the point of view of being practical and feasible, because it would require no more administration than the present collection. But then we want to find out, of course, in giving this exemption, who are

we really going to help? We can certainly And out very quickly how many this would help. We will take into consideration the man most in need, namely the man with four children. I take that example because four children give the maximum exemption allowed. The man with four children would have to earn more than $4,600 a year in order to get any benefit whatsoever from the change from our present ceiling to no ceiling. He would pay no tax at all today with his $2,000 exemption. I looked up the tax statistics of Canada and I find that 87 per cent of the taxpayers of Canada last year earned less than $4,500, a year. Actually 94 per cent of the wage and salary earners of Canada earn less than that. For them therefore this would mean no change. Let us look at the remainder. Who are the remaining people? I suppose you could call them the upper middle brackets and the rich. The upper middle brackets are not going to get much benefit. The man earning from $4,500 to $6,000 or $7,000 is not going to get much benefit because in the first tax bracket he pays only 18 per cent and in the next tax bracket he pays 21 per cent. They are not going to get much relief on such a thing. Let us look at the other end of the scale, the rich man, the man who under our present graduated income tax system, plus the 20 per cent surcharge, finds himself in the top bracket paying 96 per cent tax, if the income is earned, or 100-8 per cent if it is unearned; that is if it is solely from dividends, and interest and rents. Well, a man like that who has worked hard all these years in accumulating the money and who is now probably worrying about losing that money and is now getting on in years, will generally have plenty of real or imaginary ailments. He will have the benefit of the very best medical advice, and probably his doctors will advise him to go south, to California, to Florida, or to some European spa, to rest in expensive sanatoria. His present total exemption for these costs is $2,000, $1,000 if he has no dependent children, and at that age he is not likely to have any. Everything above that he pays himself out of his residue of income. If there is no ceiling, however, he could go on a $10,000 junket to some fine sanatorium in Arizona for five or six months, and spend $10,000 there in approved medical and hospital bills; it would actually cost him only $400 net. The remainder of $9,600 would be money which otherwise would have been collected from him by the Department of National
Income Tax Act
Revenue as income tax to go into those measures so dear to the heart of the hon. member, such as family allowances, pensions and so forth.

speechtext:
I should like to say that, with regard to the ceiling, while I agree to some extent with the parliamentary assistant, and also with the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre, nevertheless these ceilings do create in some cases great injustices. But I am forced to admit that the elimination of those ceilings would also lay the whole situation open to many abuses which the parliamentary assistant enumerated.
I must agree with the mover of this resolution, Mr. Speaker, that the present definitions in the act are too narrow. Any family with growing children is bound to have medical expenses which are a heavy drain on the family budget. These axe ordinary year to year expenses occasioned by the everyday illnesses with which unfortunately we are all afflicted. However, the matter on which I want to speak today is not in connection with these ordinary and expected expenditures. I should like to speak for a few minutes about the situation which arises when any member of a family is stricken with what amounts to a major illness, particularly if that illness results in surgery.
The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) discussed the tax situation as it affects the taxpayer earning $3,600. I believe he mentioned too that the example he gave would be of a taxpayer with two children. He would have a tax exemption for medical expenses of $1,500, and would be forced to deduct from that $1,500 ceiling the four per cent of net income, or $144. So that instead of having an exemption of $1,500 for medical expenses, he would have an exemption of only $1,356. He would have the exemption, too, only if he produced receipts for these amounts, and indicating
Income Tax Act
that the indebtedness had been incurred and the money paid within the twelve-month period.
The mere fact that the indebtedness was incurred does not give the right to tax exemption. The bills must be paid before the exemption can be claimed. We will suppose that the taxpayer in question incurred medical expenses to the extent of $1,500. Unless he has savings, his income of $3,600 will not permit his paying a medical bill of $1,500 in any one year. Therefore he is forced to spread the payment of the expense over a period of perhaps three years.
What happens? He can deduct in each year only the part he pays in that year. But before he can make the deduction he must take off in each year-not just the first one- four per cent of his income. In other words if he has a major expenditure of $1,500 which he is forced to pay over a period of three years, instead of losing four per cent of his income he loses 12 per cent. In other words he loses four per cent every year for three years. It is clear, then, that on the $1,500 medical expenses he is allowed to claim, not $1,356, which would be the amount if it was all paid in one year, but only $1,068.
If this taxpayer has a good job, or has any security he can put up, it is possible that he can borrow the money from the bank or from some other source. But any borrowing he does results in interest charges, and those interest charges are not deductible, but are personal expenses which he must assume, himself.
Quite apart from the position in which he finds himself in respect of the payment of medical expenses for which he can produce actual receipts, we must consider those nondeductible expenses, some of which have already been mentioned. I refer to expenses incurred by the family by way of transportation costs to and from the hospital, and other necessary expenses. If the person who is ill happens to be the mother, then the services of a housekeeper must be secured so as to take care of the family, and particularly if there are small children.
As has been pointed out, this always results in increased food costs, and increased costs of all kinds within a domestic establishment. Then, one must consider the purchase of medicines which are not included in the act as amended last year. I refer to medicines which are purchased and not, as the parliamentary assistant suggested, charged on hospital bills. No exemption can be claimed for them. Then there are such things as

Income Tax Act
ambulance fees. I have known some cases when an allowance has been made for them, but there are many others where they are not allowed. And in these days, when there is a shortage of hospital space and people are begging for beds, it has become the practice of hospitals to release patients as soon as it is felt they can be returned to their homes safely. In many cases they are returned home while still requiring constant attention.
In that event a nurse-sometimes two of them-would be required to look after the patient in the home. So long as the nurse is serving in the hospital the charge for her board is placed on the hospital bill. However, when she enters the home to care for the patient, no allowance is made for food, and this can be a fairly sizeable amount, particularly with food costs as they are today.
Hon. members who have preceded me in the debate made some comment about funeral expenses. Here again I should have liked to see the resolution broadened to include that item. I agree with the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre, however, when he says that by putting too much in a resolution one is more likely to have it defeated than if the scope is kept within narrow limits.
I have known cases, however, where young women receiving modest salaries have supported a parent or parents through long illnesses incurring heavy expenses, only to have the parent or parents die. Such young women are left with heavy medical expenses still to be paid. They are left with funeral expenses and, more than that, in the following years during which they will be paying off those heavy bills they find their status reduced from the married to the single state. We know that, while a young woman may be single, if she has been supporting a parent she is entitled to exemption as a married person. The result is therefore that instead of the $2,000 exemption she will have an exemption of only $1,000. The same would apply to a widow or widower.

Yes, in the following year; but when the bills are heavy they are not able to pay them in one year. Whether it be a single man or woman left with these bills, whether it be a widow or a widower, he or she is faced with a reduction of status to that of a single person, and a loss of $1,000 by way of exemption, while at the same time assuming heavy bills.
Then I would call the attention of the house to the case of the chronic sufferer, the person
TMrs. Fairclough.]
who goes through many years of life suffering from some ailment necessitating the purchase of expensive medicines. It is true that the act was amended last year to permit an exemption in respect of some expensive drugs commonly used. There are still many people however who require constant care and who use large quantities of expensive medicines which, thus far, have not been allowed as deductions under the Income Tax Act.
All these things should be considered in connection with the resolution, one which I believe should have the support of every member in the house. I do not agree with the parliamentary assistant when he suggests that the incidence of expense has anything to do with principle. The fact that there are fewer and fewer people affected has nothing whatever to do with the question as to whether or not this procedure is a just and proper one.
The parliamentary assistant referred to three briefs which had been presented during the past year, and brought attention to the fact that there had been only three. I would suggest that those three briefs covered a wide field of taxpayers. They were not the briefs of individuals. I should think that the brief of the Canadian Congress of Labour would cover a huge field of taxpayers-and taxpayers in the very bracket with which we are most concerned, namely those who are hit hardest by medical bills. I urge strongly the adoption of the resolution.

Mr. Speaker, this resolution is of special interest to me. As hon. members know, a year ago last summer I sustained severe injuries resulting from a motor car accident on a highway in Ontario. Those injuries brought me nearer to death's door than at any other time in my forty years of life.
I must say it is quite an experience to lie in hospital for five months and to consider oneself lucky to be alive while, at the same time, suffering from severe injuries requiring surgery, hospitalization and extensive medical care. During that time in hospital one has time to think, and to realize that, speaking broadly, there are three classes in the community who suffer at a time like that: Firstly, the indigent may be cared for by the municipalities, so they may not be affected to a great extent. Secondly, there are those in the middle income group; quite often these people have to draw on meagre savings when illness occurs. Then thirdly, there are those in the upper income group who do not have to face the problem with which we are concerned here.
I was quite fortunate in my own case. Being a member of the legal profession I

realized the importance of obtaining a good lawyer to look after my affairs. There was insurance on the automobiles involved in the accident and I was able to recover my expenses. But I cannot help thinking that a total of $3,500 in the way of medical and hospital expenses would be a staggering amount for some people to pay. It would be almost impossible for many people in the middle income group.
I was gratified to hear the parliamentary assistant (Mr. Sinclair) speak as he did this afternoon. I think he has done well and I think the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) has done well to give the sympathetic reception which has been given to this resolution of the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles). I am gratified further at the indication that this resolution appears to have the unanimous approval of hon. members.

subtopic: PROPOSED AMENDMENT WITH RESPECT TO MEDICAL EXPENSES

Mr. Speaker, very often I do not agree with the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) but on this occasion I do agree with him. I think he has done well to present this resolution. I want to congratulate the hon. member for Hamilton West (Mrs. Fair-clough) upon the point she made. Being a medical man I know that her remarks were absolutely to the point. I know what happens in cases of long or chronic illness.
Being a member of the medical profession practising in a rural area I know what people are up against. Doctors practising in rural areas are not served by drugstores and they must keep on hand supplies of drugs. When such a doctor is not paid for his services, he loses not only what he would charge for his medical services but also the cost of the drugs supplied. In allowing all medical expenses to be deducted both the people and the doctors would be benefited.
I think I speak for all members of the medical profession practising in rural districts when I say that they are not hard on their patients in enforcing payment of their bills. It is very seldom that they resort to the courts in an effort to have bills paid. As the hon. member for Hamilton West has indicated, they know there are many families who just cannot pay these bills. Once again I want to commend the hon. member for having brought this matter to the attention of the house.

Mr. Speaker I have only a few remarks to make on the motion now before the house; I have absolutely no intention of extending them in the least.' If I rise to take part in this
Income Tax Act
debate it is mostly because of certain comments made by the hon. member for Hamilton West (Mrs. Fairclough) on funeral expenses. I rather think that as far as these expenses are concerned, the same principle should apply as in the case of charitable donations.
Medical expenses can legitimately be deducted from our taxable income. It so happens that these expenses quite often follow a long illness which has entailed a great deal of expense.
I well understand that these funeral expenses can be deducted from the taxable portion of estates for succession duty purposes under the Succession Duty Act. In so far as his income tax is concerned, the father is protected to an extent, in that he can deduct at least part of the medical expenses incurred in the treatment of his child, but he cannot follow the same principle with respect to funeral expenses.
On the basis of that same principle, perhaps I might ask the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) to consider the advisability of amending the act so that funeral expenses could be deductible, for income tax purposes, in the same way as medical expenses.

subtopic: PROPOSED AMENDMENT WITH RESPECT TO MEDICAL EXPENSES
speechtext:
Mr,
Speaker, this matter has been dealt with at some length and there are only one or two additional points I should like to mention briefly. I refer particularly to the scope of the so-called "medical expenses". I think that the scope is unduly narrow, both for the reasons which have been put forward in the debate this afternoon and for one or two others which I shall mention. I do not pretend that these reasons are new because I have raised them myself and I am sure that other hon. members have raised them in previous sessions.
Parliament has recognized within the definition of medical expenses in the Income Tax Act that deductions should be allowed for certain aids, such as aids to hearing. The much more common aids to sight in the form of glasses are not considered as coming within the scope of medical expenses. I say today, as I have said in previous discussions of this matter in earlier sessions, that it is not fair

Income Tax Act
that spectacles and eyeglasses should not be included within the scope of medical expenses.
This type of expense falls quite heavily on some families. There are some families which because of weaknesses in eyesight are faced with considerable expense for many members of the family, and yet in no ease does the Department of National Revenue recognize expenditures on aids to sight as falling within the scope of medical expenses. That seems to me to be most unfair.
We took a step forward when we acknowledged that aids to hearing should be included. If we admit the principle of including aids to hearing, by what logic can we exclude aids to sight? A very specious answer was given a few years ago by Mr. Ilsley when he was minister of finance to the argument I put forward. He looked up the act and ran his eye down to the marginal note which then read "unusual medical expenses", not "medical expenses", as it does now. He came up with the answer that "unusual" meant unusual in nature, and as glasses were very common, therefore they could not be included within the scope of unusual medical expenses. That was a very far-fetched attempt to answer.
We are not faced with that nonsense in the new Income Tax Act. The marginal note reads simply "medical expenses". In any event the present Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) has been much fairer on this subject. When I raised this same matter a couple of years ago he acknowledged, and quite properly so, that when the expression "unusual medical expenses" was used in the marginal note in the Income War Tax Act it meant unusual in amount, namely, in excess of the old five per cent and lately the four per cent, of income, but not unusual in nature.
In approaching this question fairly, therefore, there is no reason in logic why spectacles and eyeglasses should be excluded from the scope of medical expenses.
The second point has to do with drugs. The distinction drawn here is well known to the house. If drugs are prescribed by a physician and included by him in his account, as is the case with most physicians practising in rural localities, the cost of such drugs is admitted by the department as a medical expense. But where a prescription is filled by a druggist, as would be the case with the prescriptions of most city physicians, then the department does not recognize the cost of the drugs as being a medical expense. There is no logic or sense to that distinction. We were reminded today by the parliamentary assistant that if the drugs are supplied in hospital and put on the hospital bill, then

the cost of the drugs will be recognized just as in the case of a rural physician who does his own dispensing. But by what logic do you exclude drugs that are prescribed by a physician who does not fill his own prescription?
The only answer that has ever been put forward in this house on behalf of the government has been that it would present some administrative difficulty, apparently on the theory that druggists who would certify the account for the drugs would perhaps stretch the facts in a good many cases. I have enough confidence in the druggists of this country, and I am looking at a couple of them on the other side of the house now, to believe that, when a druggist certifies, as he would be required to do, the receipted account stating that the drugs were sold in pursuance of a physician's prescription, the certificate should be respected. For the life of me, I cannot understand how the department can justify the blanket exclusion of all such expenses. It seems to me that in a case like that the taxpayer who has incurred perhaps very substantial expenses for drugs should certainly be entitled to bring those outlays within the scope of his medical expenses.
Let no member of this house think that this may be a very small matter, because for many people, particularly those who are sufferers from chronic ailments, the cost of drugs can be very large indeed. I hope that the members in this house have not had too much personal experience in this matter. If they have had an experience of illness in their families involving the prescription of drugs, they will know very well that it does not take long for the expenditure on drugs to exceed the expenditure incurred in connection with the services of the physician.
If you recognize the principle of admitting medical expenses as a deduction, and then acknowledge within the scope of medical expenses drugs which are furnished by a physician or those which are furnished by a hospital, there is no justification for excluding them in the case of those taxpayers whose prescription has been sent to the druggist to be filled there. Those are only matters of common justice, common equity, and no amount of talk about administrative difficulties or distrust of druggists can justify the injustice in those cases.

speechtext:
The little bit of special pleading which, quite frankly, I should like to do under this resolution, caused me some worry at the start as to whether it would be in order under the terms of the resolution. But in view of the discussion which has taken place this afternoon, I think it is.
The basic purpose of exemption, as I understand it, is to protect those of our taxpayers who may be seriously upset in their budgetary calculations by a sudden attack of sickness with its consequent expense. With that objective I do not believe there is the slightest disagreement anywhere in the house. In its effort to achieve that objective, the government has not been entirely successful. In a district such as the one I represent, those who are the most hard hit in proportion to their incomes and their circumstances are those whom, I admit quite frankly, it will be most difficult for the legislation to cover adequately. My little criticism is in connection with the definition of what is an allowable medical expense. If one were to say that it was an unusual expense caused as a direct result of sickness, then I would not have to raise my particular plea.
I am concerned with those who live in small, isolated communities, and who live many miles and sometimes many days from medical attention. When they are met with unexpected needs for medical attention, the destruction of their budgetary plans is sometimes out of all proportion to the seriousness of the illness which overtakes them. I think perhaps a classical example is one which came to my attention two or three years ago on the Queen Charlotte islands. A man suffered from an infected tooth, and it was essential that he get to a dentist. He got to the dentist and had his tooth pulled at a total cost of either $5.50 or $6; that was his medical expense. To get to the dentist and back cost him over $55, not counting anything for living expenses during the time he waited in the city between boats. This was a small case. Larger cases, and unfortunately there are many of them, are those where the victims of sudden illness or injury have to be flown to medical attention. The cost of such an aeroplane trip is of course never a small item. I realize that there is considerable difficulty in allowing as a deductible item the actual travelling costs incurred in getting medical attention. At the moment, I do not refer to hospitals, but in getting to doctors or dentists.

Income Tax Act
If the purpose of this exemption is going to be carried out, I would urge the parliamentary assistant to consider once more this particular angle. I know, Mr. Speaker, that it could, under certain circumstances, lay itself open to abuse. I know that there are great difficulties from the administrative angle, but I submit respectfully to those who are responsible for preparing the budget that administrative difficulties alone is not an adequate defence.

Naturally, I welcome that fact with real enthusiasm. I note that, in addition to the acceptance of the resolution which the parliamentary assistant to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Sinclair) has indicated, it has had support from other members of the Liberal party and likewise from members of the Progressive Conservative party. My friends to the left in the Social Credit party, who have refrained from speaking because they did not want to talk out my resolution, have indicated to me that they support it, and every member of my group does likewise. That seems to make it unanimous.
I want to say, Mr. Speaker, that I realize full well that the passing of this resolution does not mean the immediate legislative enactment of what it asks for. The resolution asks for all that a private member, under the rules of this house, can ask for, namely that the government give consideration to the proposal that the four per cent floor in connection with medical expenses in relation to income tax, should be wiped out. I take it that if this resolution is passed, since it has won the support of the government, the government will do what the resolution asks, namely will give consideration to that proposal. Naturally I hope the fact that this resolution is passed unanimously by this house will suggest to the government that that consideration should be favourable. I shall certainly await with interest the section of the minister's budget speech dealing with this matter, when he makes that speech on the night of April 8.
The point that this resolution asks for I think has been made crystal clear in . the debate that has taken place this afternoon. Other points have been mentioned and I hope they will be taken under review as well. I

refer to the point raised by the hon. member for Skeena (Mr. Applewhaite) and the various points raised by others who have taken part in the debate. The particular point that the house is voting on is the request that the four per cent floor be wiped out.

As the parliamentary assistant has pointed out, as I pointed out very clearly in my opening speech, and as he suggested by quoting something the hon. member for Spadina (Mr. Croll) had said to him privately, the wiping out of the four per cent floor is the provision that will be of most direct and most immediate help to those in the lower income tax brackets so far as medical expenses are concerned-at least so far as you can deal with the matter in terms of income tax relief. I earnestly hope that the consideration to be given by the government will be favourable and that we shall see the result of that consideration when the budget comes down on April 8.
