subtopic: PROPOSED CONFERENCE TO CONSIDER NATIONAL POLICY

speakeroldname: Mr. H. W. Herridge (Kootenay West) moved:
subtopic: PROPOSED CONFERENCE TO CONSIDER NATIONAL POLICY
speechtext:
That, in the opinion of this house, the government should consider the advisability of calling a federal-provincial conference on conservation with a view to the establishment of a national policy on soil, forest and water conservation and land use for Canada.

He said: Mr. Speaker, I was pleased to see the parliamentary assistant to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Sinclair) accept the resolution moved by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) and which has just been adapted unanimously by the house. I suggest that if the Minister of Resources and Development (Mr. Winters) can see fit to take similar action with regard to the resolution that I am supporting at the present time, the government will be taking action that will make it easier and easier as the years go by to grant greater and greater exemptions from income tax to the lower income tax groups.
In recent years we in Canada have begun to heal, to some extent, the scars made in our land by the exploitation of our natural resources, but we have not done nearly enough. In my opinion we are proceeding far too slowly if we are going to prevent the continual drain of our renewable natural resources. Without resources of water, timber, and minerals; without dependable supplies of food from good soils; without freedom from floods, dust storms and the wasting of water, our nation cannot remain either strong or great.
It is with that conviction, Mr. Speaker, and with that belief that I present this resolution to the house and urge the government to consider the advisability of calling a federal-provincial conference on conservation with a view to the establishment of a national policy on soil, forest and water conservation and land use for Canada.
Quite recently I was reading some old political history and I came upon what I thought was a profound statement by that great statesman and philosopher of a bygone period, Edmund Burke. I found that he once said that a great unwritten compact exists between the dead, the living and the unborn; that we leave to the unborn a colossal financial debt, perhaps inescapable; and that such an inviolate compact requires that we leave to the unborn something more than debts and depleted natural resources. From that reference, Mr. Speaker, we can see that even in the 17th century period those thinkers who thought in advance of the great majority of the people realized that there was a growing depletion of natural resources in England at that time.
Strangely enough, man is the only organism known that lives by destroying the environment indispensable to his survival. In some cases parasites may tend to do this, but their effectiveness for destructive purposes is largely limited because of the
Conservation
absence of intelligence. I repeat that man is the only organism known1 that lives by destroying the environment indispensable to his survival.
Man uses his brain, in many instances, to tear down the environment that supports him. It is only rarely, historically or geographically, that he has learned to stabilize or to rebuild his environment; and only in recent years, to any extent, has he done so. The more civilized man has become, on the whole, the more destructive he has been generally speaking when dealing with the balance of nature and maintaining the balance of renewable natural resources. Wind, water, earth and vegetation have accomplished, between them, during geographic history, the complex system which we term the balance of nature, and which man throughout the years largely has destroyed in his struggle for survival.
Men of the Stone Age left very few scars on the face of nature; but with the advance of civilization, as I said before, the steady deterioration of renewable natural resources has substantially taken place. To such an extent was this so even in the early days of man's history that we find that the prophet Jeremiah, in 550 B.C., said:
Many shepherds have destroyed my vineyards . . . they have made my present lot a desolate waste. . . the whole land is made desolate because no man layeth it to heart.
What the prophet was speaking of in this instance was the destruction of the pastures of the Holy Land through over-grazing by goats and sheep. By this time-in the time of the prophet Jeremiah-the process by which many later civilizations have been weakened, or overthrown, or have disappeared, was fully illustrated.
North China itself, although agricultural since two thousand years before Christ, must originally have been pasture land since ancient manuscripts give indication of that fact. Without a doubt, all China was once well forested.
If you read history carefully, you will find that Greece might have retained her vitality if the original 68 per cent to 70 per cent of mountain forest land had not been drastically reduced to build the great long ships that were used by the Greeks in the Mediterranean. Today less than one-twentieth of Greece is tree covered, and a great deal of the rest of it is almost incapable of cultivation. Poor land usage in every province of the Roman empire contributed to its decline and fall. Owing to deforestation and erosion, not one of the Mediterranean harbours of Asia Minor is any longer commercially useful.
The Libyan and Tunisian deserts, where in 1942 the desert armies fought for water holes

Conservation
100 miles apart, was once the African granary of the old Roman empire. The peasants of India had more food per person three hundred years ago than they have today. In Europe during the middle ages forests were denuded and great erosion commenced as a result of over-pasturing. In fact, in reading history, I find that there are two factors, two actions that have caused a great deal of erosion and loss of soil for agricultural purposes. First is the over-cutting of timber and second is overpasturing.
In Great Britain by 1600 an historian feared that the English woods must disappear within a century because the iron smelters were using so much oak charcoal. In Spain the establishment of the wood industry and the building of huge fleets, such as those that fought the armada, ruined great areas of land and started the Spanish empire on its decline.
Coming to our own continent, North America, we find that when new lands were settled in the 16th century the colonists practised careless destruction of renewable natural resources by the destruction of forests and by poor agricultural practices. By the time railways and cities had been built across the western plains of the United States, much of northern Wisconsin and Michigan was reduced to sandy stump lands. In the old south, persistent cotton cropping wore out and washed away the best soil areas of the coastal states.
Destructive practices in agriculture, lumbering and mining in the United States were I think graphically illustrated and climaxed about the year 1934 when in a single huge sand storm in the great plains of the United States 300 million tons of soil were lifted and moved in less than twenty-four hours.
Canadian experience has been very similar. Destructive lumbering practices in the early days denuded much of eastern Canada of the best forest resources. Unplanned and unscientific development of the prairies laid millions of acres waste and until recent years in British Columbia the forest resources were being rapidly depleted without any consideration for the future. Modern industry depends upon raw materials which are found at or near the earth's surface, the product of unknown ages, and for the most part they are not being reproduced by any natural processes, owing to man's carelessness and man's neglect. Anyone willing to study the literature on this subject, and it is a most interesting literature, will learn many tragic facts from these authorities about formerly fertile hillsides now turned into barren rock, about once irrigated plains now desert, and flourishing civilizations now buried beneath the sands. They will learn that this process,

which devastated Asia and North Africa centuries ago, still continues at the present day in many parts of the western hemisphere, including Canada.
The history of mankind, so far as natural resources are concerned, up to recent years has largely been one of destruction, of waste and consequent desolation. Even as early as 1887 this matter was beginning to concern thoughtful people in Canada. The drifting of prairie soil was the cause of concern to some farsighted Canadians, and in that year a committee of the Senate was established to give consideration to this problem, and the use of the natural resources of Canada. I find on looking over the records of this house that a similar committee of the Senate examined this subject in 1907.
The history of the conservation movement in North America is comparatively brief. It may be said to have been commenced when the late Theodore Roosevelt summoned a conference at the White House in 1908, of the representatives of the states, cabinet members, members of the congress, justices of the supreme court, and many other distinguished men from across the United States. At that conference a declaration of principles was adopted and steps were taken to promote joint action by the federal and state governments, because at that time it was thought effective action could only come as a result of co-operation between the federal government of the United States and the various states of that country.
Following this the late President Roosevelt, recognizing that the principles of conservation of resources are international in scope, invited the representatives of Mexico and Canada to meet at Washington in a joint North American conference, and I understand Canada sent observers to that conference. The conference further endorsed the declaration of principles of the first-called conference, and because I think they are worth placing on the record, Mr. Speaker, I am going to read them to the house. They are as follows:
We recognize as natural resources all materials available for the use of man as means of life and welfare, including those on the surface of the earth, like the soil and the waters; those below the surface, like the minerals; and those above the surface, like the forests. We agree that these resources should be developed, used and conserved for the future, in the interests of mankind, whose rights and duties to guard and control the natural sources of life and welfare are inherent, perpetual and indefeasible. We agree that those resources which are necessaries of life should be regarded as public utilities, that their ownership entails specific duties to the public and that, as far as possible, effective measures should be adopted to guard against monopoly.
I may say, Mr. Speaker, that anyone reading this declaration of principles would think

it was written by members of the C.C.F. We in this group agree wholeheartedly with this declaration of principles. It is outlined in terms that we can support fully. I would say that in fact it is a declaration of sound principles. It was not given effect but its purpose was defeated over and over again because in the United States throughout the years, vested interests have been more concerned with profits than with the development of natural resources according to the terms and principles of this declaration. There is improvement in recent years.
As a result of the conference called by the president of the United States, and as a result of proceeding erosion, soil drifting and flooding of various rivers in Canada, the question of conservation became of greater and greater concern to many Canadians, to a number of organizations, and also to various Canadian governments, so that this parliament gave consideration to the whole question in 1909 and passed an act to establish a commission for the conservation of natural resources which received royal assent on May 19, 1909, and by an order in council on the following September 3, 1909, appointed the commission. That was the first major step in Canada with respect to an over-all approach to the question of the conservation of natural resources in this country.
It might be of some interest to the hon. members at this time to know that the father of the present hon. member for Kamloops, the Hon. Frederick John Fulton of Victoria, who was at that time chief commissioner of lands for the province of British Columbia, was appointed as one of the members of the commission established as a result of the act of this parliament. However, owing to the fact that Mr. Fulton could not agree with the railway policy of the British Columbia government of the day, of which he was a member, to guarantee bonds to the tune of $40,000 per mile for the construction of a railway through British Columbia, now the present Canadian National railway to Prince Rupert, he resigned from the government of British Columbia at that time and later as a consequence resigned from the commission on conservation established by an act of this parliament.
As a long-time resident of British Columbia, I remember very clearly the vigorous debate concerning the railway policies of the late Sir Richard McBride's government. While Mr. Fulton felt bound on principle to resign from the government, I must say in fairness to him that he blazed a trail for the development of conservation policies in British Columbia, which has not been
Conservation
recognized by many people outside that province, and is not known to a good many people who reside in the province.
Under Mr. Fulton's stewardship was established the first commission in British Columbia to give consideration to the conservation of forest resources, and for the first time in British Columbia history consideration was given to the conservation of other natural resources. He was responsible for first recommending to a government of British Columbia a system of forest management licences in that province. It is only in recent years that a system of forest management licences has been established as a result of the very excellent report made by Mr. Justice Sloan, who was the royal commissioner on forest conservation a few years ago.
I think this long delay in giving effect to policies that were advocated by a farseeing man in 1906, 1907 and 1908 indicates how long it takes to build up public support for policies that are necessary and that are advocated first by men of vision and of pioneer thought.
The conservation commission functioned from 1909 to 1921. In 1921 it was abolished by an act of parliament. I read a good many of the reports of this commission. I think they did a magnificent job. It is evident from the reports, which are well worth studying, that they made a comprehensive review of the whole situation so far as renewable natural resources are concerned in Canada. Various dominion government agencies have been giving consideration to conservation throughout the years. They include the international joint commission. At this point I want to say I think we are most fortunate in having as the head of that commission the present General McNaughton, who is a first-class scientist, a first-class administrator and a gentleman who is paying strict attention to making certain Canadian interests are protected in every respect.
We have the fisheries research board of Canada, the international fisheries commission, the international Pacific salmon commission. In fairness one should mention that the former member for New Westminster, the present Senator Reid, has done very good work as a member of that commission for Canada.
The royal commission on dominion-provincial relations gave some thought to this question, to a limited extent, although it did not make any lengthy recommendations on the subject. Then, we have had various branches of the old department of mines and resources that did some work along these

Conservation
lines. Within the scope of legislation under its control, the Department of Agriculture is practising conservation of waters under the Prairie Farm Rehabilitation Act.
The Department of Resources and Development is doing very good work at the moment. The national film board has played a very capable and useful part in developing an understanding and appreciation of the necessity for the use of conservation principles in the development of our natural resources.
In addition, there have been various provincial government agencies and various departments of provincial governments, including provincial game commissions, working on various problems, as well as the work carried on by all the universities across Canada. A great deal of publicity is being given, particularly by certain weekly newspapers that appeal to the farming population. In this connection I would refer, too, to magazines published for farmers, the forestry industry, sportsman and other magazines of that type that, throughout the years, have given a great deal of publicity to the need for a policy of conservation in this country.
In addition to government agencies there has been a great deal of interest on the part of organizations of the people, the type of interest which always produces excellent results. When the people interest themselves in their own problems they usually get something done. The Canadian forestry association, which has had a long life, planned the first forestry congress in 1906, which was called at the instigation of the prime minister of Canada. This organization has done a vast amount of work for the development of policies that would result in the conservation of our forest resources, the discussion of forestry problems across the country, and an understanding of those problems.
The agricultural institute of Canada has taken a great interest in the conservation of soil and water resources, and the proper utilization of farm lands, and has suggested a national policy on soil and water conservation, and land use.
I might point out that first we had the Canadian forestry association suggesting a national congress. We had the agricultural institute of Canada suggesting a national policy on soil and water conservation and land use. Then in 1941 we had a further development as a result of public interest in this important matter. In that year the Canadian conservation association was organized, and representatives from most of the provinces were in attendance. This organization has

done some very effective work in this connection. The Canadian Federation of Agriculture throughout the years has taken a vital interest in these problems. The professional forest engineers association, the game and fish organizations in all the provinces, the rod and gun clubs, Ducks Unlimited, the men of trees organization, the women's institutes- all these have done good work. Then, the work of Jack Miner is known internationally, in connection with the habits of migratory birds.
The Canadian Congress of Labour has been interested in this subject throughout the years, and has passed resolutions indicating concern of the workingman in industry in respect of conservation policies. Only today representatives of the Trades and Labour Congress of Canada met representatives of the government, and included in their representations one for the development and conservation of our natural resources. The report of the congress had this to say in part:
We also hold it imperative that our natural resources be conserved in order that the most efficient use may be made of them now and in the future. We especially urge your government to protect the salmon fishing grounds in the west coast areas, as well as our resources of iron, oil, and forests. We request full protection of all Canadian fishermen, and fishing rights in all waters.
Canadian chambers of commerce, industry and many other organizations have been interested in this matter throughout the years. And so we have in Canada the groundwork laid for a great movement that will be concerned about greater development, so far as conservation in this country is concerned.
Realizing the work done by governments, by industry, by organizations, and by individuals in Canada, I was a bit shocked when, taking up the issue of September 13 of the Family Herald and Weekly Star, I saw the following news item:
Dr. Taggart, Not Pessimistic
"I am not one who takes too seriously the pessimistic view that we are in danger of exhausting our soil resources or that we may face hunger," said Dr. J. G. Taggart, Deputy Minister of Agriculture for Canada, when he addresed the directors' luncheon on agriculture day at the Canadian National Exhibition. He added that we must have conservation measures but that we "do not need to radically change our farm practices to save our soil and ourselves."
This is so contrary to much popular thinking that Dr. Taggart proceeded to buttress his proposition that the Canadian farmer is doing at least as good a job as any other class in our economy. He pointed out that the history of agricultural development in any new region starts with the exploitation of the soil. As population increases, practices change to conserve the soil and increase productivity. He instanced western Europe where crop yields reached a low ebb but. in the past 100

years, have almost doubled, largely due to good soil practices and the large use of commercial fertilizer.
I was greatly surprised when I read that article because, as I read it, it means that the deputy minister is not over-concerned about the depletion of our soil resources. It would seem that the condition according to him would be permitted to develop to a certain point, and then we would spend much greater sums to bring those resources back to fertility and to their former condition. To my mind that is a somewhat unusual position for a gentleman like the deputy minister of agriculture to take, in view of the representations made by agricultural institute of Canada, which has had a committee dealing with this subject for two or three years. That committee is composed of some of the best agricultural scientists in this country, who are highly qualified to deal with the problem.
I wish now to make a few suggestions as to how conservation can be made more effective by government action. The conservation of renewable natural resources covers a vast field and many diverse problems which in my opinion require co-operative efforts for success. Conservation, which means simply wise management and the wisest utilization of our natural resources in perpetuity, will become effective only when its principles become a part of the thinking of every person working on the land and in the woods, or with the products thereof. In my opinion, to accomplish this purpose the government has a basic responsibility. And when I say "government" in this connection I include dominion, provincial and municipal governments, because all human activity as expressed by government organizations affects either the management or the utilization of one or more of our renewable natural resources.
Therefore if we are going to have effective action, it requires now-not years from now -that the federal government should give effective leadership, so that there will be co-ordination, direction and guidance. I believe the federal government should give leadership in establishing standards. There are several things the government can do. Because of its central authority, it could give leadership by calling in other governments with a view to stimulating interest in national conservation.
I shall deal with only a few of the actions it could take. First of all, it should establish standards for the conservation of our natural resources. The time has arrived for co-operative action by dominion and provincial governments to establish those standards. It 55704-53
Conservation
is the obvious responsibility of this government to establish sound standards of management and utilization of natural resources, as a result of scientific advice and investigation. It should establish those standards for the proper cropping and protection of our forest resources, for the establishment of soil management and soil use standards, for sound grazing policies, and so as to have co-ordinated plans for irrigation, flood control, navigation and power development, as well as a policy for preventing the erosion along the banks of our rivers and streams. That is the first essential. What are we aiming at? What are our standards in respect of these aspects of conservation? Government must set the target.
Then the next important matter is that of research. Another obvious responsibility of governments, both federal and provincial, is to encourage and to finance research work in the conservation field, and to co-ordinate these activities with the work of public organizations and individuals.
At this point I wish to say that I think we are most fortunate in having, in our Minister of Resources and Development (Mr. Winters), a man with the advantages of youth, energy and scientific training, as well as having at heart the interests of the people. He has all the attributes required to take effective action along the lines I am suggesting.
I think we are also fortunate in our deputy minister of resources and development. Major General Young is a gentleman with a first-class mind and possessing great administrative and organizing capacity that has been proven. I am sure that if he were given the opportunity through action taken by this government we would see our conservation policy move at a faster pace and develop at a greater rate.
I was glad to note from a communication I received from the deputy minister that the department already has concluded agreements with four of the provinces for the sharing of the costs of taking a forest inventory. That is an excellent first step. When you consider the action that has been taken since the present forestry act came into effect I think you will agree that the minister deserves credit for giving effect to this legislation at a little faster rate than some other ministers have done and a lot faster than some of the ministers have done who have had control of natural resources in the days gone by.
I think the governments, both federal and provincial, should give some guidance in the way of education. The government should develop a co-ordinated educational program

Conservation
aimed at developing the interest and co-operation of all Canadians from early school days on. Every Canadian hoy and girl should be engrained with an appreciation of the value of the natural resources of this country. I think the government could do a lo't in obtaining the co-operation of the departments of education across Canada as well as of the universities. There should be a wider measure of co-operation among the universities, the departments of education and all government agencies directly responsible for the application of natural resources policies.
I think more publicity should be given to the work of the Department of Resources and Development. This is a most important department of government under present conditions. When we think of the work of the minister's officials and scientists, the highly trained men working in the engineering and water resources branch, in the administration of lands division, in the parks division, in the forestry branch, in the forestry research division, in the forest operations division, in the forest products laboratory and so on, we realize how little people know of the good sound work being done throughout the years.
I am reminded of a poem which I memorized about 1906 when I was a boy. I think of two lines of Gray's "Elegy in a Country Churchyard," when I think of the work done by these scientists and highly trained men which goes unnoticed and unsung. The lines I remember are:
Full many a flower is born to blush unseen,
And waste its sweetness on the desert air.
More should be done to give publicity to the work of the department. I think much could be done by the national film board to popularize this matter. The co-operation of the press could be obtained to a greater extent. Then finally is the question of law enforcement. I think there would be great advantage in dominion-provincial co-operation in the establishment of uniform law enforcement. This uniform law enforcement could apply also to the shooting of game and other wildlife, the catching of fish, and trapping.
There is great need at this time for the co-ordination of all the activities of government at all levels along with public organizations, various provincial departments and other organizations such as I have mentioned already. We should get the farmers, the labour organizations, industry, the women, the technical organizations and the youth of this country working together with understanding to support a co-ordinated national conservation policy.

In conclusion I would suggest that the estimates of the Department of Resources and Development should be submitted to the committee on mines, forests and waters, not from a critical standpoint but so that the members of that committee would have an opportunity to call in the officials of the department and learn more about the excellent work being done. I think it would be of value to hon. members to hear from the minister and his officials of the work that has been done, that is being undertaken and that is being proposed.
In my opinion members of this house and the Canadian people generally are insufficiently informed of the importance of the work being done by this department. I believe in the urgency and importance of this matter and therefore I have spoken at some length. May I close with an earnest plea for recognition by the members of this house of the great need for some action at this time. There have been centuries of universal waste and the time has come in Canada to set up a national policy for the conservation of our natural resources based on the principle of co-operation between the dominion and the provincial governments and all the people of Canada.

speakeroldname: Hon. Robert H. Winters (Minister of Resources and Development):
subtopic: PROPOSED CONFERENCE TO CONSIDER NATIONAL POLICY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the resolution proposed by the hon. member for Kootenay West (Mr. Herridge) urges the government to consider the advisability of calling a federal-provincial conference on conservation with a view to the establishment of a national policy on soil, forest, and water conservation and land use for Canada. This is perhaps one of the most important subjects that this house could deal with. At the outset I wish to thank the hon. member for the kind things he has said about the officials of the Department of Resources and Development. I am sure they will be grateful to him for that encouragement.
In reply to his suggestion that the people of Canada should be given a greater opportunity to know what the department is doing, perhaps I should take this opportunity to review some of the fields in which this department and other departments of government have been working in an effort to bring about a greater conservation of Canada's renewable resources.
I doubt if there is any difference of opinion throughout the country as to what this policy should be. There has been a sequence of conferences, both between federal and provincial governments and among other groups concerned with this problem, stretching back for many years, and there have been many

speeches and statements by leaders of all political parties and by representatives of industry, forestry associations, farmers and many others on this matter. Running through all these has been unanimity that our policy in regard to forest, soil and water resources- all of which are renewable resources-must be to encourage their best utilization consistent with maintaining them on a sustained yield basis. That is, we must see to it that the annual depletion of these resources, whether by cropping or by wastage through fire, flood or disease, is not greater than their replenishment, either by natural process or by human assistance, such as reforestation, fertilization, etc.
There is a wide general knowledge, too, of the interrelation of our various natural resources with each other. I think it is generally understood that the degree of forest cover affects the speed of the water run-off and the level of the water table in areas far distant. A fast run-off can cause floods that will wash away thousands of acres of fertile soil and will result in a disastrous shortage of water at other times of the year. Falling water tables make it harder and harder to get water needed for cattle, agricultural irrigation, and household and industrial uses.
I do not think there is any lack of public understanding of the urgency for a conservation policy or of the necessity for achieving such a policy. The problem is a complex one. It stems in part from the fact that the development of resources on sound conservation standards is not always compatible with the optimum and immediate realization of profit. It is probably true that conservation does over the long run produce the maximum profit from resources, but as Lord Keynes said, "In the long run we are all dead". It may be difficult, therefore, for even the most public-spirited board of directors or individual operator to adopt, beyond a point, costly measures of development merely for the purpose of preserving our natural resources for the use of our grandchildren and great-grandchildren. They are apt to point out that these higher costs, if carried by the industry, must ultimately be borne either by the consumers of the product through higher prices or by the owners or operators of the resources through lower profits. But it is more comforting to face a future with even high-priced resources rather than no resources at all.
There is, I believe, pretty wide public acceptance of this general principle that some of the costs of conservation should be borne by the taxpayers generally, but there is room for considerable discussion on two points concerning its application. The first is the extent to which it should be applied, the 55704-531
Conservation
degree to which the taxpayer should carry the burden of conservation. The second is the determination of what proportion of the burden should be borne by private enterprise, and what should be carried by the taxpayers of the province on the one hand and by the taxpayers of the whole country on the other. In other words, how much of the government contribution to conservation costs should be made by the provincial and municipal governments concerned, and how much by the federal government. Problems such as these are usually best solved by dealing with each case on its own merits, rather than by trying to lay down general principles because the surrounding conditions tend to vary so widely from case to case.
As hon. members realize, the federal government has assisted, and does on many occasions assist, the provincial governments in conservation projects. It may be helpful if I refer to some of the more important recent occasions, and the principles on which the federal government participated. I shall deal only with those projects concerning forestry and flood prevention, because the matter of soil conservation is more appropriately a matter for my colleague the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner). I need only mention the valuable service to Canada rendered by the minister and his department through the medium of the Prairie Farm Rehabilitation Act and the Maritime Marshland Rehabilitation Act. The latter has already paid dividends in my own part of the country.
First I should mention what has been done under the Canada Forestry Act. This act was passed in 1949 and provides, among other things, for the federal government to enter into agreements with any province for the protection, development or utilization of forest resources. Of course defence expenditures must be given priority, but the importance the government attaches to this matter of conservation was indicated when on May 2, 1951, I was able to announce in this house that the federal government was prepared to enter into agreements with the provincial governments for completing reliable forest inventories and in encouraging reforestation. I pointed out at that time that a forest inventory is essential before a sustained yield policy can be successfully planned. It is impossible to determine whether your stock position is improving or worsening unless you know what your inventory is from time to time. I stated then *that reforestation is badly needed in certain areas which will not regenerate themselves naturally, and where forest cover is necessary

Conservation
not only for the development of forest products but also in the interest of floor control, soil conservation, et cetera.
Forest inventory agreements have been signed during the fiscal year 1951-52 to date with six provinces

New Brunswick, Ontario, Manitoba, Saskatchewan, Alberta, British Columbia. They are five-year agreements, under which the federal government agrees to pay to the provinces 50 per cent of the cost of completing inventories of the provincial resources, and 50 per cent of the cost of maintaining the inventories when completed. Three of the six agreements-those with Ontario, Saskatchewan and British Columbia-include agreements for undertaking reforestation. In addition, a reforestation agreement has been signed with Prince Edward Island.
These agreements provide that the annual federal contribution to each province for reforestation will be equal to either 20 per cent of the province's expenditure for this purpose or the amount by which the provincial expenditure for the current year exceeds the average for the past three years, whichever is the lesser; and in addition the federal government will pay 20 per cent of the cost of the establishment of any new provincial forest nursery.
When planning these agreements a federal-provincial conference was held in May, 1951, and was attended by forestry officials from each of the ten provinces and from the federal government. It is expected that a similar conference will be held in the not too distant future to consider future programs.
Other fields in which the federal government has made valuable contributions to forest conservation are forestry research and forest products research. Forestry research is carried on in Ottawa and through five district offices and five forest experimental stations situated in different regions throughout the country. It covers silviculture and forest management, forest inventories, and fire protection research. Such research is essential toward providing solutions to many problems encountered in improving forest management.
Forest products research is undertaken in two forest products laboratories, one in Ottawa and one in Vancouver. It covers such fields as wood utilization, wood preservation, timber mechanics and wood chemistry. There is in addition an experimental sawmill in Ottawa. The importance of forest products research should not be overlooked, because if conservation is to be thorough it must not

be limited to the growing forest, but must cover the utilization of all parts of the tree, the preservation of wood and wood products, the substitution as far as possible of more common woods for those less common, and so on.
I would also like to mention the work of the eastern Rockies forest conservation board. This board was established in 1947 by agreements between the government of Canada and the province of Alberta. It has jurisdiction over an area of more than 8,600 square miles covering the upper portions of the South Saskatchewan river and its tributaries. Briefly stated, the purpose of the board is to protect and develop these lands so as to maintain the most desirable conditions for watershed management. It is hoped thereby to reduce the peak of flood waters in the spring and maintain the maximum flow during the summer. The agreement covers a period of twenty-five years and provides among other things for the expenditure of $6,300,000 voted by the parliament of Canada for capital improvements during the first six years. The agreement also provides for an annual appropriation, not exceeding $300,000, for maintenance and other current expenditures.
In this connection, too, we must not forget the value of the national parks, particularly those in the Rocky mountains, in conserving the forest cover which protects the watersheds of some of Canada's most important rivers.
I am sure that hon. members will expect me to say a word about the valuable role being played in the field of conservation by private enterprise. Many of our leading manufacturers of pulp and paper today, as well as the enlightened operators of sawmills, have already achieved sustained yields in their forestry operations. Because of large timber limits required, sustained yield is not always possible, but the spirit of progress and enlightenment is certainly permeating the field. Private enterprise now forms one member of the team with governments in the over-all field of conservation for the benefit of our generations as yet unborn. I would like to say more about what is being done to develop and conserve Canada's resources, but, since it is six o'clock, I move the adjournment of the debate.
Motion agreed to and debate adjourned.
